subject: history_social
passage: In the 1850s, British engineers building a railway between Lahore and Multan, in what is now Pakistan, needed ballast, the crushed material packed under rails to keep them steady. Near the village of Harappa they found a ready supply: mounds of old fired bricks, which laborers broke up and spread beneath the track. Only decades later did archaeologists realize that the mounds were the remains of a city of the Indus civilization, more than four thousand years old. By then much of the upper part of the site had been carried away, and the archaeologists who excavated Harappa in the 1920s had to work with what the railway had left.
stem: Based on the text, why was the excavation of Harappa in the 1920s more difficult than it might have been?

choices.A: The laborers who broke up the bricks refused to reveal where they had found them.
choices.B: The archaeologists did not know that the mounds belonged to the Indus civilization.
choices.C: The engineers had built the railway line directly across the center of the site.
choices.D: Much of the ancient city had already been removed for use under the railway tracks.

explanation.why: The text explains that the bricks from Harappa's mounds were broken up for ballast, and that "by then, much of the upper part of the site had been carried away," so the archaeologists "had to work with what the railway had left behind." The difficulty was the loss of material from the site.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says nothing about laborers refusing to share information.
explanation.B: Incorrect. By the 1920s archaeologists had realized what the mounds were; the text says this happened "decades later" than the 1850s, before the excavation.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the bricks were taken from the mounds and spread under the track; it does not say the track ran across the site.
explanation.D: Correct. The text states that much of the upper part of the site had been carried away for ballast before the 1920s excavations.
